paradisiacal.meaning: Like a perfect place; perfectly happy and beautiful.

ragamuffin.meaning: A poor child in old clothes.

hobbledehoy.meaning: A boy who is not yet a man and who moves in a way that is not nice to see.

destitution.meaning: The state of being so poor that one has no food or home.

apoplectic.meaning: Red in the face and almost ill with strong feeling, such as anger or laughing.

menagerie.meaning: A group of wild animals kept together.

sere.meaning: Dry and dead, as grass is in the fall.

tares.meaning: Bad plants that grow among the food plants and hurt them.

sheaf.meaning: A group of plants cut and held together.

relinquish.meaning: To give up something that one has or hopes for.

teutonic.meaning: From the land of the Germans.

paragraphs.context: “Boys. I want to open a school for little lads
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jo says that the crop she will grow at Plumfield is boys. She wants a happy, homelike school, with Fritz to teach them.
paragraphs.simple: Laurie asks what the fine crop is to be. Jo says it is boys. She wants to open a school for little boys. It will be a good, happy, homelike school, with her to care for them and Fritz to teach them.

paragraphs.context: Yes; Jo was a very happy woman there, in spite of hard work, much anxiety
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jo is very happy at Plumfield in spite of hard work and noise. She has two little boys of her own, who grow up well among the crowd of schoolboys.
paragraphs.simple: Yes, Jo was a very happy woman there, in spite of hard work, much worry and constant noise. She enjoyed it fully. She found the praise of her boys more satisfying than any praise from the world, because she now told stories only to her flock of eager believers and admirers. As the years went on, two little boys of her own came to make her happier. They were Rob, named for grandpa, and Teddy, a carefree baby who seemed to have his papa's sunny temper as well as his mother's lively spirit. How they grew up alive in that whirlpool of boys was a mystery to their grandma and aunts. But they did well, like dandelions in spring, and their rough nurses loved and served them well.

paragraphs.context: Touched to the heart, Mrs. March could only stretch out her arms
paragraphs.mainIdea: The book ends with Mrs. March holding out her arms to her children and grandchildren and saying she cannot wish them a greater happiness.
paragraphs.simple: Mrs. March was touched to the heart. She could only stretch out her arms, as if to gather her children and grandchildren to herself. With a face and voice full of a mother's love, thanks and humility, she said, 'O, my girls, however long you may live, I never can wish you a greater happiness than this!'

sentences.context: Nothing could be more natural or proper than for my Professor to open a school, and for me to prefer to reside on my own estate.
sentences.simple: It is the most natural and right thing for my Professor to open a school and for me to like living on my own land.
sentences.grammar: 'Nothing could be more ... than for X to ... and for Y to ...' is a way to say 'it is the most ... thing'. The two 'for ... to' parts name two actions that Jo calls natural.

sentences.context: I hope there will be more wheat and fewer tares every year
sentences.simple: I hope there will be more wheat and fewer weeds each year.
sentences.grammar: 'More ... and fewer ...' compares two amounts. 'More wheat' and 'fewer tares' use a picture from a farm to talk about good and bad in a family.

sentences.context: Into each life some rain must fall
sentences.simple: Some rain must fall into every life.
sentences.grammar: The verb comes after the object phrase for a poetic order: 'Into each life ... must fall'. In normal order it would be 'Some rain must fall into each life'.

try one's hand at.meaning: To try to do something new, to see if you can do it.
try one's hand at.example: He’ll try his hand at it there

lay up.meaning: To save something, such as money, for later.
lay up.example: laying up the blessings of the poor, instead of dollars
